stories.headline: Teen arrested in fatal Denver shooting near Tower Road
stories.summary:
A 17-year-old boy is in custody after a Tuesday afternoon shooting in northeast Denver left one man dead, according to the Denver Police Department. Officers responded to the 5800 block of Tower Road at about 5 p.m.

Investigators believe the teenager was arguing with the man before shooting him. Police have not publicly identified the boy because of his age. He was later arrested in the 5800 block of North Ceylon Street, less than a mile from the shooting and roughly 5 miles from Denver International Airport.

Paramedics took the man to a hospital, where he died. The Denver Office of the Medical Examiner will identify him. Police did not describe the relationship between the man and the teenager.

The case remained under investigation Tuesday. Charges had not yet been filed by the Denver District Attorney's Office, and police said the story was developing.

stories.headline: Update: Judge dismisses lawsuit against Amendment 87; appeal to Colorado Supreme Court expected
stories.summary:
A Denver District Court judge on Wednesday rejected a last-minute effort to remove Amendment 87, the graduated income tax measure, from the November ballot. The ruling lets the proposal remain before Colorado voters.

A Republican activist filed the lawsuit against the Colorado Secretary of State's Office in September. The suit argued the initiative should not have been placed on the ballot because dozens of paid signature gatherers did not follow the state's registration rules.

The case is expected to reach the Colorado Supreme Court before Election Day. Advance Colorado, a group that opposes Amendment 87, also backs a competing measure, Proposition 136, which would cap income tax rates.

The dismissal marks a significant development after earlier court hearings on the challenge. Amendment 87 would change Colorado to a graduated income tax system.

stories.headline: RTD projects $148 million deficit in proposed $1.34 billion 2027 budget
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District expects a $148 million deficit for fiscal year 2027 on a proposed budget of $1.34 billion. The agency projects $1.19 billion in revenue, and its board will consider adopting the budget on Dec. 1.

RTD says it has cut the deficit from $282 million in fiscal 2024 and aims to eliminate it by 2028. Officials cited reviews of service delivery costs, administrative and contractual spending, and staffing. The agency also refinanced debt, saving $20 million.

Proposed operating costs are $915 million, a $206 million decrease from fiscal 2026 before East Colfax Bus Rapid Transit expenses. RTD plans $615.2 million in capital spending, including the Downtown Rail Reconstruction Project, expected to finish next year.

Tax revenue of $940 million would make up 79% of projected funding, with RTD relying heavily on a 1% sales tax. An agency spokeswoman said the structural deficit cannot be fixed through revenue growth alone.

stories.headline: Nederland pitches new financing structure for Eldora Mountain Resort purchase amid resident backlash
stories.summary:
Nederland is proposing a new financing structure to buy Eldora Mountain Resort after bondholders rejected its original plan. The Boulder County ski area was the subject of a $225 million bid.

Many residents say it is time for the town to walk away from the deal. Trustees have also raised concern that ending the bid would mean losing $2.5 million already put down.

The outcome could shape the future of one of the Front Range's closest ski areas and the finances of the small mountain town.

stories.headline: KeyBank CEO bullish on Denver despite population loss and downtown struggles
stories.summary:
KeyBank's chief executive says he sees growth ahead in metro Denver despite stiff competition among banks. The bank's deposits in the market increased by more than $150 million.

The CEO, Chris Gorman, expressed confidence in the region even as Denver deals with population loss and a struggling downtown.

The comments offer a read on how a large regional lender views the Denver market amid those pressures.

stories.headline: SMOK barbecue owner to open Baja-inspired Mexican stall in Boulder
stories.summary:
Bill Espiricueta, who has run the Michelin-recommended Denver barbecue restaurant SMŌK since 2018, is opening a new Mexican concept in Boulder. Costa Brisa debuts Nov. 2 on the first floor of Avanti Food & Beverage's Boulder location, at 1401 Pearl St., in the former Quiero Arepas space.

The menu focuses on Baja-inspired dishes such as shrimp tostadas, a California-style burrito with carne asada, cheese and French fries, and Baja fish burritos. It also includes tacos, quesadillas and bowls. On weekends it will offer SMŌK's popular breakfast burrito.

Espiricueta said Baja fish tacos he tried at SMŌK drew a strong response and inspired the concept. He previously ran Vaca Gordo in Denver. Costa Brisa will be open Thursday from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Friday and Saturday from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.

stories.headline: Frank Bonanno opens Italian-Japanese restaurant Rōmyō in Larimer Square
stories.summary:
Denver restaurateurs Frank and Jacqueline Bonanno opened Rōmyō in mid-September at 1401 Larimer St. The restaurant serves itameshi, a Japanese style of cooking that uses Japanese ingredients in Italian dishes. The name combines Rome and Tokyo.

The menu includes a chawanmushi egg custard with a parmesan-based dashi and a Chitarra alla Sake that swaps sake for vodka in an Abruzzo red-sauce pasta. Other dishes use truffles, bonito flakes and Ibérico pork. Colorado ingredients include soy sauce aged in Leopold Brothers whiskey barrels.

Booths along the edges of the space are designed to resemble train cars, with screens acting as windows showing Japanese and Italian countryside. Bonanno began his Denver restaurant career in 2001 with Mizuna and has said some dishes will evolve as he works through them.

stories.headline: Colorado highway traffic cameras go offline statewide
stories.summary:
Live traffic cameras along Colorado's highways and interstates went offline Wednesday night because of an unknown problem, the Colorado Department of Transportation said. Both live video feeds and still photos were unavailable on cotrip.org and the COTrip app.

CDOT issued the alert at about 6 p.m. and said it was working toward a solution, without providing further details on the cause.

The COTrip map showed a scattering of cameras still online, but most feeds along Interstate 70 and Interstate 25 were absent as of 7 p.m.

stories.headline: Prescribed burns at Rocky Mountain Arsenal send smoke across Denver metro area
stories.summary:
Smoke was visible across the Denver metro area Wednesday as firefighters conducted prescribed burns at the Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge. Aurora Fire Rescue confirmed the large plume visible on Aurora's north side came from the controlled burns.

The burns took place near East 56th Avenue and Memphis Street in Commerce City. Ignition was scheduled to begin at about 9:30 a.m., with operations potentially continuing until 5 p.m.

The refuge warned residents of a possible smoky odor and urged the public not to call 911 about the smoke. Wildlife Drive and trails remained open during the burns.

stories.headline: 49th Denver Film Festival opens Thursday with about 150 titles
stories.summary:
The 49th Denver Film Festival opens Thursday, Oct. 22, with a screening of "I Play Rocky." About 150 additional titles will screen through closing night on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Venues include the Ellie Caulkins Opera House, Sie FilmCenter and the Denver Museum of Nature & Science. Tickets were still available for the recommended titles but are trending toward sellouts.

Local interest titles include "The Ascent," about Colorado Springs climber Mandy Horvath's effort to crawl up Mount Kilimanjaro, and "Cheyenne," about female bronc riders. The festival's guests include actor John Cho, who will receive the Outlaw Award, and Indya Moore. Passes and individual tickets are available at denverfilm.org.

stories.headline: Nuggets open 2026-27 season at Oklahoma City with same starters and new pieces
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets open the season Thursday in Oklahoma City with the same starters and several new pieces for coach David Adelman, who begins his second full season. The team again starts with an open roster spot.

Jamal Murray, an All-Star and All-NBA selection last season, is expected to see a managed workload. Christian Braun's $125 million extension takes effect, raising his salary to $21.6 million after an ankle sprain limited him last season. Cameron Johnson remains on a $23 million contract that expires after the season, and Aaron Gordon's soft-tissue injuries remain a concern.

The roster additions include DeRozan and Bagley, according to the Gazette preview. Nikola Jokic has said he will sign a new long-term deal in the summer of 2027.

stories.headline: Avalanche reach 10-game mark at 5-4-1 after two poor performances
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche reached the 10-game mark of the 2026-27 season Tuesday night at 5-4-1, after back-to-back poor performances against Philadelphia and New Jersey. Coach Jared Bednar said he was not happy with the last two games but called the start "not horrible."

The Avalanche are plus-11 in goal differential. Last season's team started 5-1-4 before winning 31-2-7 on the way to a franchise-best 121 points, while the 2022 champions started 4-5-1.

Defenseman Josh Manson said the team should not compare itself to last year's start, calling it an anomaly. The team enters its next 10-game segment looking to correct the issues from the recent losses.

topStory.headline: Rogers and El-Sayed Clash Over Trump, Loyalty and Policy in Final Michigan Senate Debate
topStory.summary:
Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed met Wednesday night in the second and final debate of Michigan's increasingly bitter U.S. Senate race, which aired on WXYZ-TV. The candidates answered questions on manufacturing and Canadian tariffs, immigration enforcement, health care and the war with Iran. The exchange was somewhat tamer than their first debate earlier this month, which featured insults and interruptions in nearly every answer, but it remained testy.

El-Sayed, a former executive director of the Detroit Health Department, repeatedly argued that Rogers, a former congressman, would be a "sock puppet" for President Donald Trump. He described Rogers' platform as a "MAGA vision" and said his opponent stands "hip-to-hip" with Trump on policies he said are raising gas and grocery prices. El-Sayed also invited the audience to play "MAGA bingo" in response to Rogers' attack lines. Rogers replied that the bingo game should be counting how many times El-Sayed mentions Trump in an answer. After the debate, Rogers told reporters he planned to attend a Trump rally in Michigan on Sunday, though he said final details were not yet known.

Rogers accused El-Sayed of a "pattern of deception" about his platform and said many Democrats were declining to support him because he is "too extreme." He also claimed El-Sayed was aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America and wanted bigger government and higher taxes. El-Sayed describes himself as a capitalist and is not a DSA member, though he is backed by several members of the group, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who campaigned with him in the Upper Peninsula last week. Opening statements reflected each side's central theme: Rogers cited lost manufacturing jobs and high utility and auto insurance rates, while El-Sayed pledged to lower the cost of living.

The most contentious moment came when Rogers questioned whether El-Sayed, a Michigan-born Muslim who would be the first Muslim elected to the Senate, is loyal to the United States. Rogers tried to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group founded in Egypt, and said he had donors who supported Iran-backed groups such as Hamas and Hezbollah. "Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked. El-Sayed called the attack "shameful," said he is proud to be an American, and rejected the allegations. He has repudiated the Brotherhood and noted he was not raised by his birth mother after his parents divorced. The charges followed reports earlier this month on social media posts by his half sister suggesting his mother had supported the group, and came amid false claims by Trump that El-Sayed is a "jihadist."

The race is neck and neck and is among the most closely watched contests of the November midterms, with the potential to help decide control of the Senate. Democrats hope to capitalize on Trump's low approval ratings and voter frustration over inflation and the Iran war, while Republicans are seeking to exploit divisions between progressives such as El-Sayed and moderate Democrats over Middle East policy and Medicare for All. With no further debates scheduled, both campaigns now turn to the final stretch before Election Day, including Trump's planned Sunday rally in the state.
